Concrete cost per square foot

A standard residential concrete slab costs $6 to $12 per square foot installed in 2026, with most projects landing near $8. Here is exactly what makes up that number — every line, every rate, and what pushes a project to the high end.

Regional pricing

Concrete cost varies by region

Ready-mix pricing tracks local construction volume, fuel costs, and plant competition. Labor moves the installed price even more.

On installed cost, the Northeast adds 15–25% and the West Coast 20–35% versus the Southeast and Midwest. Island and remote sites can push ready-mix past $250 per yard.

Why prices differ

What pushes a quote up or down

Site access

If the truck can back up and chute the concrete in, there is no extra charge. If the pour is in a backyard, uphill, or past a fence, you need a pump — $450 to $900 minimum, rising with volume. Wheelbarrow-only access adds $1–$2 per sq ft in labor.

Ground condition

Poor soil needs engineering fill, extra compaction, and deeper excavation. This can add $1–$2.50 per sq ft, and it is the first place to look when a bid seems high.

Slab size

Small slabs carry more fixed cost per square foot. A 10 x 10 pad runs $8.50–$15.00 per sq ft; a 40 x 60 driveway runs $6.50–$12.50. The rate drops because delivery and crew setup spread out.

Removal and haul-off

Tearing out an old 4-inch slab runs about $4 per sq ft to demo and haul, more as it gets thicker. Often the second-biggest line item after labor.

How much does a concrete slab cost per square foot?

A standard residential concrete slab runs $6 to $12 per square foot installed in 2026, with most projects landing near $8 per square foot. That figure includes ready-mix concrete, delivery, a compacted gravel base, forms, reinforcement, placing and finishing labor, control joints, and curing compound — but not major excavation, permits, or decorative finishes.

The cost per square foot breaks down roughly like this:

  • Concrete material: $2–$3.30 per sq ft
  • Labor (pour and finish): $3–$8 per sq ft — usually the single biggest line
  • Site prep and forms: $1–$2.50 per sq ft
  • Reinforcement: $0.20–$2.00 per sq ft
  • Curing and sealer: $0.25–$1.00 per sq ft

Small slabs cost more per square foot than large ones because the truck delivery, crew minimum, and forms are fixed costs spread over less area. A 10 x 10 pad typically runs $8.50–$15.00 per sq ft, while a 40 x 60 driveway lands closer to $6.50–$12.50 per sq ft. Decorative work — stamped, colored, or exposed aggregate — adds $3 to $10 per sq ft on top.

One important caveat about scope. Published per-square-foot figures disagree by nearly 40%, and the reason is that they measure different things. A quote at $6 per sq ft is often scoped to exclude delivery fees, control joints, curing compound, and site prep — real costs that a complete project pays. Price the same scope before comparing two bids; a lower number is not a better deal if it is missing items.

How much does it cost to pour a concrete slab?

Pouring a concrete slab costs $4 to $14 per square foot installed, depending on thickness, reinforcement, finish, and how much site work the ground needs. A plain broom-finished 4-inch slab on a flat, accessible site sits at the low end; a thick, reinforced slab on ground that needs grading and fill sits at the high end.

Realistic totals for common sizes at $6–$12 per sq ft:

  • 10 x 10 pad (100 sq ft): $600–$1,200
  • 12 x 12 pad (144 sq ft): $864–$1,730
  • 20 x 20 slab (400 sq ft): $2,400–$4,800
  • 24 x 24 garage pad (576 sq ft): $3,500–$9,000
  • 30 x 30 slab (900 sq ft): $3,600–$7,200

A useful shortcut: the concrete itself is only about 25% of an installed slab. Labor is usually 45–55%. That is why a slab quoted at $4 per square foot for materials alone is not out of line — it simply excludes the crew.

How many bags of concrete do I need?

Divide the pour's volume in cubic feet by the finished yield of one bag, then round up. Standard yields are 0.30 ft³ for a 40 lb bag, 0.45 ft³ for a 60 lb bag, and 0.60 ft³ for an 80 lb bag.

Bags = ceil( volume in ft³ x (1 + waste%) / yield per bag )

One cubic yard of concrete equals about 90 bags of 40 lb, 60 bags of 60 lb, or 45 bags of 80 lb mix.

Worked example — a 10 x 10 ft slab at 4 inches thick:

  • Volume = 10 x 10 x (4 ÷ 12) = 33.3 ft³ = 1.23 yd³
  • With 10% waste: 36.7 ft³
  • 80 lb bags: ceil(36.7 ÷ 0.60) = 62 bags
  • 60 lb bags: ceil(36.7 ÷ 0.45) = 82 bags

Bagged mix stops making sense above roughly 1 cubic yard. Past about 45 bags of 80 lb mix, hauling, mixing, and pouring by hand costs more in time and labor than a ready-mix truck — and cold joints between batches are far more likely.

How many yards of concrete do I need?

Multiply length by width by thickness in feet, then divide by 27. There are 27 cubic feet in a cubic yard.

Cubic yards = (Length ft x Width ft x Thickness in ÷ 12) ÷ 27
Shortcut: Cubic yards = (sq ft x thickness in) ÷ 324

For a 20 x 20 ft slab at 4 inches: (400 x 4) ÷ 324 = 4.94 cubic yards. Add 5–10% for waste and order about 5.5 yards.

As a rule of thumb, one cubic yard covers about 81 sq ft at 4 inches, 65 sq ft at 5 inches, 54 sq ft at 6 inches, and 41 sq ft at 8 inches. A standard ready-mix truck carries about 10 cubic yards.

How thick should a concrete slab be?

Spec it by load, not by rule of thumb:

  • 3.5–4 in — walkways, garden paths, patios, shed and AC pads (foot traffic only)
  • 4 in — the standard residential minimum; patios and light floors
  • 5 in — residential driveways and garage floors carrying passenger cars or half-ton pickups
  • 6 in — driveways taking trucks and RVs, heavy equipment pads, and commercial slabs
  • 8 in — post-tensioned, heavily loaded, or industrial slabs

For code: the International Residential Code (R506.1) sets a 3.5-inch minimum for slab-on-grade floors in habitable space, and most jurisdictions amend that to 4 inches. The IRC does not regulate exterior patios and walkways, though local codes often do govern driveways — published driveway standards run from 4 to 7 inches depending on the municipality.

ACI 330R-08 puts it plainly: "As a practical matter, there is no benefit in building slabs less than 4 in. (100 mm) thick." Thickness is the cheapest structural upgrade available — bending capacity scales with the square of thickness, so 4 in to 6 in is 50% more concrete but roughly 2.25x the bending resistance.

What PSI concrete do I need for a slab?

Match the strength to the exposure and the load:

  • 3,000 PSI — interior slabs, basement floors, and shop floors that never see salt or freezing
  • 3,500 PSI — standard patios, sidewalks, and exterior residential work
  • 4,000 PSI — driveways, garage floors, and any exterior slab in a freeze-thaw climate, specified with 5–7% air entrainment
  • 4,500–5,000 PSI — heavy vehicle pads, warehouse slabs, and structural work per ACI 318

ACI 332 requires 4,000 PSI with air entrainment for exterior residential slabs in freeze-thaw zones. Each 500 PSI step up adds roughly $4–$10 per cubic yard, which is cheap insurance against scaling and spalling. In freeze-thaw climates, air entrainment matters more than an extra inch of thickness — 3,000 PSI slabs without air can scale badly within 5 to 10 years.

What makes up the cost of a concrete slab per square foot?

For a standard 4-inch residential slab installed in 2026, the money divides roughly like this:

  • Concrete material — 20–30% ($1.98–$2.50 per sq ft at $155–$160 per yd³)
  • Placing and finishing labor — 45–55% ($3.00–$8.00 per sq ft)
  • Site prep, excavation, and forms — 10–20% ($1.00–$2.50 per sq ft)
  • Reinforcement — 2–15% ($0.20–$2.00 per sq ft)
  • Control joints, curing, and sealer — 3–8% ($0.25–$1.00 per sq ft)

The most common misconception is that the concrete is the expensive part. It is not — labor is. That is why a DIY project is genuinely cheaper: you are not buying the 50% of the cost that is crew time.

It also explains why size changes the per-square-foot price. Delivery, crew minimums, and form setup are fixed costs, so they weigh heavier on a 100 sq ft pad than on a 1,000 sq ft driveway.

How does thickness change the cost per square foot?

The concrete portion scales linearly with thickness. At $160 per cubic yard:

  • 4 in — $1.98 per sq ft of concrete, 81 sq ft per yard
  • 5 in — $2.47 per sq ft, 65 sq ft per yard
  • 6 in — $2.96 per sq ft, 54 sq ft per yard
  • 8 in — $3.95 per sq ft, 41 sq ft per yard

Add 10% for waste and those become $2.17, $2.72, $3.26, and $4.34.

Because total cost per square foot includes fixed and variable parts, going from 4 to 6 inches raises the total per square foot by less than 50% — the labor and delivery do not double. A 6-inch slab typically lands $1.50–$2.50 per sq ft above a 4-inch slab, not 50% more.

How much more does decorative concrete cost?

Decorative finishes add roughly $3 to $10 per square foot on top of a standard slab:

  • Smooth trowel — $0.75–$2.00 per sq ft
  • Exposed aggregate — $2.50–$5.50 per sq ft
  • Stamped — $5.00–$10.00 per sq ft
  • Polished / ground — $6.00–$14.00 per sq ft

Stamping roughly doubles the finishing labor, which is why a stamped patio can cost as much as the structural slab beneath it. Add $1–$3 per sq ft for color, and a stain or sealer on top.

Budget against the high end. Decorative work is the least forgiving place to cut corners, because a misaligned stamp cannot be corrected without replacing the slab.

How much does a yard of concrete cost?

Delivered ready-mix runs $130 to $180 per cubic yard in most U.S. markets in 2026, with 3,000 PSI mix around $135–$160 and 4,000 PSI around $143–$180. The ready-mix industry's own benchmark survey puts the average selling price near $160 per yard.

Four published supplier price lists read in October 2026 showed 3,000 PSI at $127.05–$165.00 per yard and 4,000 PSI at $132.00–$175.00 before tax.

Small orders cost more per yard once trip fees land. A single yard delivered runs $195–$295; 6 yards runs $870–$1,170; a full 10-yard truck runs $1,450–$1,950. Suppliers commonly add a $50–$200 short-load fee on orders under 4 to 5 yards.

Regional spread: the Southeast runs $125–$145 per yard, the Midwest $135–$155, the Southwest $140–$160, the Northeast $155–$180, and the West Coast $165–$195.

How much does concrete weigh?

Normal-weight structural concrete weighs about 150 pounds per cubic foot. One cubic yard — 27 cubic feet — therefore weighs roughly 4,050 lb.

That is why concrete arrives by truck: a single yard of finished concrete is over two tons, and a full 10-yard load weighs about 40,500 lb.

Other densities you may run into:

  • Normal weight: 145–155 lb/ft³ (typical ready-mix)
  • Lightweight: 90–120 lb/ft³ (used where a lighter slab is needed, such as over a soft sub-base or on an upper floor)
  • Heavyweight: 180–200 lb/ft³ (radiation shielding — rare in residential work)

For a 20 × 20 ft slab at 4 inches, that works out to about 20,000 lb of concrete in the finished slab. Weight is also a planning factor for pump trucks and for confirming that a crew and equipment can handle the pour.

How much does concrete cost per square foot in 2026?

A fully installed residential concrete slab runs $6 to $12 per square foot in 2026. The PourCost model produces a typical figure of $11.04 per square foot for a 20 x 20 ft slab at 4 inches with a base, forms, mesh, labor, joints and curing.

The spread is not sloppiness — it is scope. At the $6 end you are usually looking at concrete and placing labor only, with the base, forms, reinforcement, control joints, curing compound and site prep all excluded or billed separately.

At the $12 end you have a thick base, proper forms, rebar, a difficult access, or a decorative finish.

The single most useful thing to do with a per-square-foot price is check what it includes before you compare it to another one.

How much does the concrete material alone cost per square foot?

Concrete material alone is about $2.00 to $3.30 per square foot at 4 inches thick.

The arithmetic: one cubic yard covers 81 sq ft, and ready-mix runs $135 to $175 per cubic yard in 2026. So each square foot costs roughly $1.70 to $2.20 in material, and adding a 10% waste allowance brings the material-only figure to about $2.00 per square foot.

At 6 inches thick, where one cubic yard only covers 54 sq ft, the material cost rises to roughly $2.75 to $3.30 per square foot.

If you see a quote that looks competitive but works out to less than $3 per square foot for materials, check whether delivery and labor are included. Most "$6 per square foot" figures are really $4 of concrete plus $2 of labor, with everything else left out.

What does concrete labor cost per square foot?

Placing and finishing concrete runs $3.00 to $8.00 per square foot, and that is usually the largest line on the bill. For the reference 20 x 20 slab, labor is $1,800 of the $4,417 total — 41%.

It is expensive because finishing is not one task. The crew has to place the concrete, screed it flat, bull-float it, edge it, float it again, broom or stamp the surface, cut or groove the control joints, apply the curing compound, and protect the slab while it cures.

The rate rises with difficulty. A flat, accessible slab with a broom finish sits at the low end. Stamped concrete, a slope for drainage, or a site the crew cannot reach with a wheelbarrow all push it up.

This is why a per-square-foot price is only meaningful when you know whether labor is in it. Concrete is commodity-priced and moves within a narrow band; labor is local, and it is where regional differences of 15–35% come from.

How much does a 10 x 10 concrete slab cost?

A 10 x 10 ft slab at 4 inches costs roughly $1,600 to $2,200 installed in 2026, with about $10.90 per square foot typical.

The material side is small: 100 sq ft at 4 inches is 1.23 cubic yards, which is 62 bags of 80 lb mix — around $400 in bags. Ready-mix for the same volume is about $190 in concrete plus a $120 delivery, and most contractors would order a full yard and have roughly a quarter yard left over.

The rest is fixed cost: forms, a base, labor to place and finish, joints and curing. A 10 x 10 slab has proportionally more form and labor per square foot than a 20 x 20, because the setup does not scale down with area.

At this size the ready-mix versus bags question usually decides the cost. Compare the two directly on the ready-mix page.

How much does a 20 x 20 concrete slab cost?

A 20 x 20 ft slab at 4 inches costs $3,200 to $4,400 installed in 2026 — about $11.04 per square foot at the typical rate.

The material requirement is 400 sq ft × 4 inches = 5.43 cubic yards with waste, which is 245 bags of 80 lb mix or two ready-mix loads. Concrete and delivery together come to roughly $960.

The other $3,400 is site prep ($340), gravel base ($500), forms ($180), reinforcement ($180), vapor barrier ($80), labor ($1,800), control joints ($175) and curing compound ($200).

Move the slab to 6 inches and you add 1.54 cubic yards of concrete — about $240 — plus more base, more rebar and more formwork. Move it to a stamped finish and add roughly $4,200 for the pattern work alone.

What does concrete cost per square foot for a driveway?

A concrete driveway runs $8 to $14 per square foot installed, above the range for a patio or pad, because it carries vehicles and is usually thicker.

A standard single-car driveway is 10 x 20 ft = 200 sq ft, at $1,600 to $2,800. A two-car driveway of 12 x 24 ft = 288 sq ft runs $2,300 to $4,000.

The premium over a patio comes from three places: 5 to 6 inches of thickness instead of 4, #4 or #5 rebar rather than mesh, and the forms and labor to hold a long narrow pour with proper joints.

There is also a length limit. A driveway should be poured in sections of roughly 10 to 12 feet, with a control joint between each. A single 40-foot pour without joints will crack across the middle, no matter how well it is reinforced.

What does concrete cost per square foot for a patio?

A patio runs $7 to $12 per square foot installed, at the lower end of the concrete range because a patio carries no vehicles.

A 12 x 12 ft patio = 144 sq ft at $1,000 to $1,700. A 16 x 20 ft patio = 320 sq ft at $2,200 to $3,800. A 20 x 20 ft patio = 400 sq ft at $2,800 to $4,400.

Patios are usually 4 inches thick, on a 4-inch compacted base, with welded wire mesh. Where the patio abuts the house, you often see a thickened edge — that is where frost and rain get in, and it is worth the extra concrete.

A stamped or colored patio adds $5 to $12 per square foot on top. The material is nearly the same; what you are paying for is the labor to stamp and seal the surface.

Why do published concrete prices per square foot disagree with each other?

Because the prices are quoting different scopes, and the difference is almost always in what is excluded rather than in what is included.

The two figures you will see most often are around $6 per square foot and around $11 per square foot. Both can be right. The $6 figure is typically concrete and placing labor only. The $11 figure adds a 4-inch compacted gravel base, forms and edge setup, reinforcement, a vapor barrier, control joints, curing compound and sealer, and site prep.

Neither is wrong; they are different products. The practical failure is comparing a scoped-out quote against a scoped-in one and declaring the contractor expensive.

When you put quotes side by side, list the same ten line items for each and compare the totals. If two contractors quote the same scope, they should land within about 15% of each other in a competitive market.
